summary: Presents a generic model and object formats for session authorization in NSIS signaling layer protocols, so network elements can authorize use of resources and coordinate signaling and transport planes. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: Showing a ticket to prove you may reserve a seat before it's held.

subtitle: Authorization tokens so routers can verify that resource requests are legitimate

tldr.problem: NSIS signaling needs per-session and per-user authorization, but without a way for clients to prove their requests are legitimate, network elements cannot distinguish authorized from fraudulent QoS or firewall rule changes.
tldr.mechanism: A SESSION_AUTH object carries authorization information from a trusted third party (an authorizing entity) that clients insert into NSIS signaling messages. Network elements verify the object's authenticity and integrity before granting resources.
tldr.outcome: Network elements can authorize resource requests at the NSIS signaling layer, supporting fine-grained admission control and coordination between signaling and transport planes.

facts.label: AUTH_ENT_ID subtypes
facts.value: IPv4, IPv6, FQDN, X.500 DN, URI, Kerberos, X.509 cert, PGP cert, HMAC-signed

today: RFC 5981 is an Experimental protocol defining authorization for NSIS signaling layer protocols. It has not been updated or obsoleted and remains available for use with QoS NSLP and NATFW NSLP.

sections.title: Authorization in NSIS
sections.content:
The Next Steps in Signaling (NSIS) framework provides signaling for QoS reservations and other network services. While GIST, the underlying signaling transport layer, can secure communication between adjacent nodes (for example, using TLS), a single GIST connection may carry signaling for many sessions from many users. To enforce per-session and per-user authorization, signaling layer protocols need a mechanism for clients to prove their requests are legitimate.

This document defines the SESSION_AUTH object, a reusable authorization mechanism for all NSIS signaling layer protocols (NSLPs). It uses a third-party token model: a trusted authorizing entity issues authorization credentials to a client, who inserts them into NSIS messages. Network elements (routers or Policy Decision Points) then verify the credentials before authorizing the request.
sections.plainLanguage: A router needs to know that you really are allowed to ask it to save bandwidth for your video call. Rather than you proving yourself to each router, an authority gives you a signed ticket you can show to any router along the path.

sections.title: SESSION_AUTH Object Structure
sections.content:
The SESSION_AUTH object contains a list of attributes that describe an authorized session. The key attributes are:

  • AUTH_ENT_ID: identifier of the entity that authorized the request (IPv4 address, IPv6 address, FQDN, X.509 certificate, PGP certificate, or Kerberos principal)
  • SESSION_ID: unique identifier for this authorization session, used to detect replays or correlate with authorization records
  • SOURCE_ADDR and DEST_ADDR: the IP addresses and optionally ports authorized for the session
  • START_TIME and END_TIME: time window when the authorization is valid
  • NSLP_OBJECT_LIST: list of NSLP objects covered by a keyed-hash for integrity protection
  • AUTHENTICATION_DATA: signature or HMAC that proves the object has not been tampered with

Multiple SESSION_AUTH objects can be included in a single message to support authorization from different entities or for end-to-end signaling across administrative domains.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket says who signed it, which routers and bandwidth you are allowed to use, when the ticket expires, and has a signature to prove nobody forged it.

sections.title: Integrity Mechanisms
sections.content:
The SESSION_AUTH object supports four integrity mechanisms corresponding to different security environments:

  • Shared symmetric keys: Both authorizing entity and router are pre-provisioned with the same key. An HMAC computed with this key protects the object.
  • Kerberos: The client obtains a ticket from the Kerberos Key Distribution Center, which is either embedded in AUTHENTICATION_DATA or exchanged separately, and optionally protected with an HMAC using the extracted session key.
  • Public key (X.509 V3 or PGP): The authorizing entity's certificate is included in AUTH_ENT_ID. The object is signed with the private key; routers verify using the public key and certificate chain validation.
  • HMAC-signed: A special AUTH_ENT_ID subtype that uses a shared key to protect the integrity of NSLP messages themselves (not just the SESSION_AUTH object). The Key-ID field identifies which key to use for HMAC verification.

All implementations must support HMAC-SHA2-256 as a minimum.
sections.plainLanguage: The ticket can be protected in different ways: with a shared secret only you and the authority know, with a Kerberos ticket, with your digital signature, or by signing the entire message with a secret key.

sections.title: Authorization Models
sections.content:
The RFC defines four deployment models adapted from RFC 3521:

  • Coupled model: The authorizing entity and the router are tightly integrated. Only a SESSION_ID is needed; the router looks it up against its own authorization database.
  • Associated model (one policy server): A Policy Decision Point (PDP) centralizes authorization for a domain. The SESSION_AUTH object carries SESSION_ID and AUTH_ENT_ID so the router can consult the appropriate PDP.
  • Associated model (two policy servers): Similar to one server, but with redundancy or per-domain policy servers.
  • Non-associated model: The SESSION_AUTH object is self-contained with source/destination addresses, time limits, and authentication data. The router makes authorization decisions autonomously without consulting the authorizing entity.

The SESSION_AUTH object can also provide integrity protection for NSLP messages themselves when HMAC-signed, allowing per-user authentication and message-level authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: Depending on the network, the ticket might be checked locally by the router, sent to a central authority, or be self-verifying with all the information the router needs built in.

sections.title: Message Processing and Error Handling
sections.content:
When a QoS or NAT/firewall NSLP message arrives with a SESSION_AUTH object, the receiving node performs the following steps:

  1. Extract the SESSION_AUTH object and verify its integrity using the indicated mechanism (shared key, certificate, or HMAC).
  2. Check that the AUTH_ENT_ID type is supported; reject if unknown.
  3. For non-associated models, verify that the source and destination addresses, ports, and time window in SESSION_AUTH match the request.
  4. Consult the authorization policy (locally or via an AAA server) to determine whether the specific request is permitted.
  5. If authorization fails, return an error response with an appropriate error code (Authorization failure for QoS, Authorization failed for NATFW).

The START_TIME field provides replay attack protection by rejecting messages that arrive long after the time specified. The SESSION_ID allows a PDP to detect replays using internal records.
sections.plainLanguage: The router checks that the ticket signature is real, that the time is right, that the addresses match what you asked for, and that your policy allows it, then either grants your request or sends an error.
